rationale: This is a small (14 KB text, 39 functions) but compute-heavy C++ template benchmark (Stepanov container/abstraction demo: bignum Fibonacci, deque/list/vector tests, introsort), so the dominant constraint is runtime overhead on hot arithmetic- and iterator-intensive loops, not size. FLA gets the highest SecurityGain/DiversityGain because the large, control-dense functions (deque_test at 1023 bytes, __introsort_loop and __copy_move_backward variants, list operations at ~900+ bytes) benefit most from flattening, but its RuntimeCost/CorrectnessRisk weights stay high so the selector avoids flattening small hot leaf templates where flattening is both costly and fragile. BCF is similar: strong obfuscation value but the highest cost weights of any pass, restricting it to functions where features indicate sufficient slack. SUB is the workhorse — cheap, correct, and effective on the arithmetic-heavy code (bignum chains, container value types) — so it has low cost/risk weights and solid gain weights, letting it apply broadly. SPLIT and IBR provide cheap diversity that composes with FLA/BCF (splitting enlarges basic-block populations for later passes; indirect branches obscure the flattened dispatch), so their DiversityGain is kept above their modest gains/costs. ICALL and IGV are moderate: this program has many direct template instantiations and C++ global/static state (vtables, functor objects) where indirection hides call targets and global references cheaply, but their RuntimeCost weights are kept mid-range since indirect calls add per-call dispatch cost in tight container loops. Overall the table biases selection toward low-cost passes (SUB, SPLIT, IGV) applied broadly, with expensive passes (FLA, BCF) gated to the few large complex functions where their security payoff justifies the overhead.
